Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National Mahama commissions $12m EXIM Bank-funded cashew factory in Techiman Source : Albert Kuzor 16 November 2026 5:58pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
President John Dramani Mahama has commissioned a major cashew processing factory in Techiman in the Bono East Region, as part of the government's efforts to expand local agro-processing, create jobs and reduce the export of raw agricultural commodities.
The NADKANSCO Cashew Processing Limited facility, which received approximately $12 million in financing from the Ghana Export-Import Bank (Ghana EXIM Bank), has the capacity to process up to 33,000 metric tonnes of raw cashew nuts annually.
At the commissioning ceremony on Monday, November 16, 2026, President Mahama announced plans to restrict the export of raw cashew nuts during the first three months of the harvesting season to give local processors priority in purchasing the commodity.
He said the measure would be modelled on a similar policy implemented by neighbouring Côte d'Ivoire to strengthen its domestic cashew processing industry.
“So when the season opens, for the first three months of the season, nobody will be allowed to export cashew nuts from Ghana until our local processors have bought enough. When they have bought enough, then we'll open the gates for the excess to go,” he said.
The President also announced plans to introduce a levy on raw cashew exports, with the proceeds channelled into a dedicated fund to support local processors in purchasing more nuts.
He explained that the proposed measures were necessary to ensure factories had adequate raw materials to operate throughout the year rather than shut down after exhausting their initial supplies.
President Mahama said the government would provide additional funding to Ghana EXIM Bank to on-lend to NADKANSCO to enable it to purchase sufficient raw cashew nuts for year-round production.
He noted that although the bank had financed the factory's capital expenditure, including machinery and equipment, the company required substantially more working capital to purchase enough raw materials.
“Exim has financed the capital expenditure, the machines and everything. And in addition, they are giving money for working capital. But if you look at the volume of cashew that we produce, you are going to need much more than $100 million to purchase enough cashew to keep this factory running all year round,” he said.
According to the President, the financing currently available to the company would sustain operations for only about 60 to 80 days.
“We don't want a factory that will run for 80 days, shut down for the rest of the year, until the next cashew season. NADKANSCO should be able to buy enough cashews and preserve it so that the young people here can have work all year round,” he added.
President Mahama said the additional support would be channelled through the agribusiness and tree crops components of the government's new economy agenda.
Chief Executive Officer of Ghana EXIM Bank, Sylvester Adinam Mensah, disclosed that the bank had committed approximately $12 million to support the establishment and operations of the factory.
He said the financing covered the acquisition of automated processing equipment, working capital and training to equip the workforce with the necessary technical skills.
More than $3 million of the funding went into acquiring the factory's automated processing equipment.
Mr Mensah said the bank supported the project because it recognised the potential of a Ghanaian-owned processing company located within a major cashew-producing area to buy directly from farmers and export processed kernels instead of raw nuts.
He said the investment was intended to demonstrate that large-scale cashew processing could succeed in Ghana while creating employment close to farming communities.
The EXIM Bank CEO disclosed that the facility had already employed nearly 1,000 people directly and supported another 3,000 livelihoods indirectly across the cashew value chain.
These include farmers, aggregators, transporters, packers and loaders.
“That is 4,000 livelihoods sustained in one decision to process here at home instead of shipping raw nuts abroad,” he said.
Mr Mensah said the factory had an installed capacity to process 100 metric tonnes of raw cashew nuts daily under a two-shift operation.
Its annual processing capacity of up to 33,000 metric tonnes is almost twice the total volume of cashew processed locally across Ghana in the previous year.
He disclosed that Ghana produced more than 262,000 metric tonnes of raw cashew nuts last year, but only about 17,000 metric tonnes were processed domestically.
“Yet only 17,000 metric tonnes were processed here at home. The rest left our shores as raw nuts, and with them went the jobs, the skills, and the value,” he said.
The factory is expected to produce cashew kernels, cashew nut shell liquid and briquettes for export, while supplying cashew cakes, briquettes and roasted kernels to the domestic market.
President Mahama said the commissioning of the facility demonstrated government's commitment to extending Ghana's agricultural value chain beyond primary production to processing, packaging and marketing.
He explained that the creation of the Ministry of Trade, Agribusiness and Industry was intended to address the challenges farmers face in finding markets for their produce after harvest.
He said farmers were often left at the mercy of traders who determined the prices of their produce, particularly when dealing with perishable commodities.
The President argued that exporting raw agricultural produce amounted to exporting jobs and wealth while importing finished products transferred employment opportunities to other economies.
He urged Ghanaian investors to take advantage of opportunities in manufacturing and agro-processing rather than concentrate on trading.
“We shouldn't only open pure water factories. We have enough pure water factories. We need factories that will process our raw materials for export. We need factories that will create jobs for our people,” he said.
He further challenged local entrepreneurs to establish industries capable of processing maize, rice and mangoes into finished products for domestic consumption and export.
“I want to see more NADKANSCOs, not only processing cashew, but processing many other things. Processing maize flour, processing rice for local consumption and export, processing mangoes for juice for local consumption and export. There's so much that we can do,” he added.
The President disclosed that government planned to invest $10 billion of its own resources in eight strategic sectors under the new economy agenda, with agriculture and agribusiness among the priority areas.
President Mahama also urged NADKANSCO and other manufacturers to take advantage of incentives under the government's 24-hour economy policy.
He said businesses operating multiple shifts could benefit from accelerated depreciation of their plants and equipment over two years, allowing them to free up cash for reinvestment.
He added that companies seeking to expand or establish new factories would enjoy deferred payment of import duties and levies on equipment for one year, with payments spread over the following two years.
The President said the incentives were intended to encourage more investors to establish factories and create employment opportunities.
He also commended Ghana EXIM Bank for its role in supporting local industries, citing its intervention in a factory project in Savelugu, which had stalled after its initial financing proved inadequate.
He said the bank provided additional financing to complete the facility, which now operates two shifts and employs more than 2,000 people, about 80 per cent of whom are women and young school leavers.
President Mahama urged NADKANSCO's management to expand its operations and ensure the factory remained productive throughout the year.
The commissioning marks another step in government's drive to strengthen domestic manufacturing, increase value addition to agricultural commodities and retain more of the economic benefits of Ghana's production within the country.
On her side, the Managing Director of NADKANSOCO, Belinda Akorfa Adokpa, says the company is positioned to "earn Ghana $40 million in foreign exchange every year at the onset," if the company operates year-round.
She also added that the company has already trained "1,247 farmers in four weeks" who are to serve the factory the needed cashew, and also, with the needed funding from EXIM Bank, the company plans to train an additional 1,000, all under phase one of capacity building.
Under phase two of capacity building, she noted that "A further 2,000 farmers across eight districts." Adding, "This factory will create 1,500 direct jobs, together with some 3,000 indirect jobs for farmers, aggregators, transportation and traders."
